## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

## The respondents

No first-person account by a German reservation agent or revenue director was found in public (no HN thread; the
site's quotes are curated testimonials). **Every person is the author's invention**, no real person's name is used,
and each is built on the public facts named here.

Reservation agents (Parts 1 and 2):
- Lena Hoffmann: a trade-fair Saturday in a Munich central office; built on YC-L ("During peak hours") and the Munich
  hotel YC-L features.
- Murat Yilmaz: a check-in rush at the desk; YC-L's "peak hours".
- Chiara Russo: a group whose call center already answers after hours (YC-C: "Even with call centers..."); her pain is
  group emails, so Importance and Current solution go against the founder.
- Jonas Weber: alone on a Sunday desk; YC-L's "On holidays" / after hours.
- Aylin Demir: an old phone system that cannot forward (Compatibility only_with_help); the author's.
- Tobias Brandl: the sceptic who will not hand guests to an AI (Relative advantage negative, Adoption no); the author's.
- Elif Kaya: weekend abandoned calls seen on Monday; YC-L's "After hours".
- Daniel Okonkwo: rates pushed wrong to agencies matter more (Importance against); the author's.
- Mehmet Arslan: a vague story, GUESSED. Katarina Novak: a story chip, GUESSED.
- Florian Gruber, Nadia Haddad: gate No (no unanswered booking call in the 7 days).

Revenue directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3): Stefanie Wagner (6%), Andreas Keller (4%, below the founder's 5%),
Roberto Bianchi (8%), Ingrid Lindholm (2%, a call center covers after hours), Karim Benali (does not know his rate;
YC-L's "Free AI Strategy Workshop" and SITE's free test number as his ask), Petra Vogel (5%), Hannes Moser (nothing,
would not pay), Joanna Wiśniewska (10% at resort hotels in high season). The value boxes are percents of the calls, in
the founder's unit and period; the price picks are two codes, the pilot's rung and the licence's rung, each placed
against the founder's €3,000 and €1,000.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

screens.why_b3: The words are recognisably my trade's, but this belief is not among those I checked, and "You said At least 8 in 10" gives me a bar I don't recall setting; my problem is calls that ring out unanswered, not calls coming in.
screens.why_b4: It sends me to the next two cards for how often and whether it matters, but never says what this result means for Codyco, and it does not warn me that it says nothing yet about missed calls.
screens.why_b5: The n is visible, the small group is called "a lean, not a call" and "Common" stays with these 7, but "Holding up" on a question nearly every reservation agent answers yes to reads a little like support for my problem when no missed call was tested.
screens.instead: A booking call came in on all 7 shifts, which only shows these agents take the calls; it does not show any went unanswered, so read the next two cards for that.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits directly beside the deciding count, 6 of 7 inside what I said against a bar of 5 of 7, so I have both the answer and the reason.
screens.why_b2: The days axis, the median at 6 and the seven people are all there, but "5 to 7 days out of 7" and "bar 5 of 7" use the same numbers for days and for people, so I need a second look to see that the bar counts people.
screens.why_b3: Frequency and 5 to 7 days out of 7 are recognisably my numbers and my reservation shift, but this line is not among the beliefs listed as checked on the way in, so I cannot call it word for word mine.
screens.why_b4: "Whether it matters is the next card" points me onward but does not say what this means for the idea, namely that calls arrive on nearly every shift, so the chance to miss one comes up almost daily.
screens.why_b5: All seven people stay visible, Tobias is shown counting against, and "a small group: a lean, not a call" keeps the result from claiming more than seven answers can carry.
screens.instead: 6 of the 7 agents had booking calls on 5 or more of the last 7 days, so calls are a near-daily part of the job for this small group, but this doesn't yet show that any went unanswered or that it matters; the next card tests that.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "6 of 7 put it in their two · bar 5 of 7", so I can see the belief held and which number decided it.
screens.why_b2: The caption is plain about 7 people and 14 picks, and my 6 stands out, but the bar and verdict count people while the strip shows 6 for and 8 against in picks with the marker at 5, so I need a second look to see that only one person, Chiara, counted against me.
screens.why_b3: The Importance title and the belief line are word for word what I checked, and the problem is named as "Booking calls that ring out unanswered".
screens.why_b4: The So line tells me carefully how to read the number (top two, not first) but not what it means for the idea or what I should do next, such as keeping missed calls as the problem to build on while testing it with more agents.
screens.why_b5: The claim stays with "these 7", the screen says "a small group: a lean, not a call", and it warns that top two does not mean ranked first, so nothing goes beyond the answers.
screens.instead: Keep the verdict, count the strip in people (6 for, 1 against, marker at 5), and end the So line with: missed booking calls are worth building on for now, but this is only 7 agents, so check it with more, including groups like Chiara's whose call center already covers the phones.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits directly above "6 of 7 said today's way falls short · bar 5 of 7", so I can see the belief held and which number decided it.
screens.why_b2: Each answer rung has its count, the line marks where falling short starts, and the strip and bar show 6 for against a bar of 5 out of 7.
screens.why_b3: The card's title and belief line are the ones I checked on the way in, word for word, and the bar is the 2 in 3 I accepted.
screens.why_b4: The So line spells out the gap rung by rung and tells me my solution is judged against it on the next study, so I know this gap is what the pilot has to beat.
screens.why_b5: The claim stays with "these 7", all seven answers are listed, the against is shown, and the small group is called "a lean, not a call".

screens.why_b1: The box opens on Holding up with 6 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, and the line 'Importance held, 6 of 7' ties the number to the verdict.
screens.why_b3: Importance and the belief line about booking calls that ring out unanswered are the words I checked on the way in, unchanged.
screens.why_b4: The screen shows the one dissent but never says what it means for Codyco, such as whether groups with after-hours call center cover are a weaker fit or what to test next.
screens.why_b5: It keeps the counts visible and shows one quote as one person, but never says 7 people is a small sample, calls a ranking choice 'said no', and leaves out Current solution without explaining why, though the two lines below the box explain Prevalence and Frequency.
screens.why_b6: Chiara's answer adds what I did not type: where a call center covers the phones after six, the daily pain moves to group requests and emails with no rates attached, which is one person's account but a real clue about who is not my buyer and what competes with missed calls.
screens.instead: Importance held 6 of 7, a small sample; the one against has a call center covering the phones after six and is busier with rate-less group emails, so ask prospects who answers their after-hours calls, and Current solution has no box here because [state the reason].

screens.why1: As the first question, it makes sense to check that I work in a hotel group's reservations setup before asking about my work.
screens.why2: Hotel group, central reservations office and call center are everyday words in my job, so I can answer on first reading.
screens.why3: I know without guessing that my employer is a hotel group running a central reservations office in Munich.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover this factual question without overlap, and the gate correctly has no escape.
screens.why5: It describes only my workplace, with no sign of a product, plan or founder's term for people.
screens.why6: It is one 18-word question with two short options that I can hold after one hearing, though "I'll read 2 options" is a little stiff for a yes-or-no question.

screens.why1: After asking whether I work in a central reservations office, it makes sense to check that I had booking calls this week before asking about a recent one, even though the answer is obvious for me.
screens.why2: Booking call and shift are my everyday words, so I can answer straight away on one reading or hearing.
screens.why3: Taking booking calls on my shift is my job, so I know for certain whether they came in during the last 7 days.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but the chip about not recalling one particular shift is odd because the question does not ask about one shift and I would know if any calls came in this week.
screens.why5: Nothing about a product or company reaches me, and the question only uses the ordinary words of my work.
screens.why6: Said aloud, it is one short question followed by yes or no, so I can answer after hearing it once.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did a booking call come in on your shift? Yes / No (no escape chips)

screens.why1: It follows naturally from the last question, but in a central reservations office booking calls come in on every shift, so it feels like counting my shifts and I wonder why it is asked.
screens.why2: Booking call, shift and days are the words I use every day, and I understand it on first reading.
screens.why3: I know which days I worked last week, and I took booking calls on all of them, so I can answer without guessing.
screens.why4: 1 to 7 covers every possible answer after I said yes on the last screen, the numbers are distinct, and I can't recall fits as the escape.
screens.why5: Nothing of a product or founder reaches me; it only asks about calls on my shift.
screens.why6: Heard once, it is one short question with a number range and a single escape, so I can just say a number.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, on how many days did you work a shift that took booking calls? (1 to 7, or I can't recall)

screens.why1: After being asked how many days calls came in, it makes sense to ask which part of my shifts I would most like made easier.
screens.why2: I understand it at first reading, and channels, check-in rush and group requests are everyday words in hotel reservations, though 'run of shifts' is slightly loose.
screens.why3: I can answer about calls, emails, rates and groups from my central office, but rates are usually set by revenue management and the desk and check-in rush belong to front-desk colleagues, so two or three options are not my own daily work.
screens.why4: The tasks are distinct and in my words and 'None of these' fits, but 'Handling guests' requests at the desk' and the check-in rush only fit someone at the front desk, and there is no plain option for simply getting through the booking calls I do answer at peak.
screens.why5: No product is named, but 'ring out unanswered' sits among the other options as the one framed as a problem, which hints a little at what the study is after.
screens.why6: It is one question with five short options I can hold and one escape, but 'getting through the check-in and check-out rush' and 'answering booking emails and group requests' are a mouthful to hear once.
screens.instead: Think of your last run of shifts. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Keeping rates right on every channel; answering every booking call at peak; booking calls after hours; answering booking emails; or handling group requests. Or say none of these.

screens.why1: After being asked about calls on my shift and what I would like made easier, it makes obvious sense to ask how answering those calls actually went on my last shift.
screens.why2: I understand it at once, but "through a central reservations office or call center" is a stiff add-on, because I work in that office and would just say "how did the calls go on your last shift?"
screens.why3: I took the calls myself on my last shift, so I know how many rang out and whether we called them back, even if the count is a feel rather than a figure.
screens.why4: The ladder is in my words and the escape fits, but "some" and "a few" blur together, the last two options overlap because "few called back" and "simply lost" are close, and a shift where the phones were simply answered with no ring-outs has to be squeezed into "answered or called back in minutes".
screens.why5: Nothing of a product or a company reaches me; it asks only about calls ringing out and call-backs, which is my own daily work.
screens.why6: It is one question and five options a listener can just about hold, but the long office phrase in the stem is a mouthful and the comma-joined options such as "some rang out, called back when there was time" are hard to keep apart when heard once.
screens.instead: Think of your last shift. How did the booking calls go? Every call answered or called back in minutes; a few rang out, all called back that day; some rang out, called back when there was time; most that rang out were never called back; or nobody called back at all. Or say someone else did it that shift.
